replace: The animal evidence is described by the same author without figures: rats with the same heroin history were more likely to survive a high intravenous dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin than the same dose given in a different environment (Siegel et al., 1982, as described in Siegel, 1984; the 1982 paper itself was not read), and setting-specific tolerance is said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named).

The one animal experiment read is in rats (Siegel et al., 1982): male laboratory rats were given 15 intravenous heroin injections in rising amounts, one every other day, always in one of two settings (the colony room, where each was housed alone, or a separate room with constant white noise), and an inactive injection of dextrose solution in the other setting on the days between, so both settings were familiar to every rat; each rat then had one high test dose (15 mg/kg; study condition) either in the setting paired with heroin or in the setting paired with the inactive injection, and death within minutes, judged by the absence of a heartbeat, was the only outcome. In the heroin-paired setting 32.4% of 37 rats died, in the setting paired with the inactive injection 64.3% of 42, and among 28 control rats that had never had an opioid 96.4% (editors' counts from the printed percentages, each of which fits only one whole number: 12 of 37, 27 of 42 and 27 of 28; a difference of about 32 in 100 and a risk ratio of about 2.0, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.3, editors' calculation), and in each of six replications more rats died in the setting paired with the inactive injection. The experiment therefore compared a place linked with the drug with a familiar place linked with an inactive injection, not a familiar place with a new one; tolerance itself was never measured, so weaker tolerance as the reason is the authors' interpretation; and the paper names no method of assigning rats to groups, reports no losses and prints no test statistics, and its p < .001 for the difference between the two heroin-experienced groups does not reproduce from its own counts (chi-square about 8.0, p about .005, editors' calculation). Setting-specific tolerance is also said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named).

Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982), as described by its author: rats given a high intravenous heroin dose in the environment previously paired with heroin were more likely to survive than rats with the same history given it in a different environment; no survival figures given.

Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982; 107 male rats, editors' sum; a single 15 mg/kg intravenous test dose after 15 rising doses on alternate days, study conditions): died after the test dose, heroin-paired setting 32.4% of 37 (12, editors' count), setting paired with an inactive dextrose injection 64.3% of 42 (27), controls with no previous opioid 96.4% of 28 (27); difference 31.9 percentage points, risk ratio 1.98 (Katz 95% CI 1.18 to 3.32), Pearson chi-square 7.98, p = 0.005 (continuity-corrected 6.76, p = 0.009; Fisher two-sided p = 0.007), against a printed P < .001 (editors' calculations); three groups printed P < .001 (chi-square 27.8, editors'), each heroin-experienced group against controls printed P < .002 (the closer one, 27 of 42 against 27 of 28: chi-square 9.8, p = 0.002, editors'); six of six replications in the same direction, printed P < .02 by a binomial test (one-sided 0.016, two-sided 0.031, editors'); median time from the start of the injection to death 187, 174 and 164 seconds, reported as not significantly different; test setting counterbalanced (17 and 20 of the 37; 21 and 21 of the 42, editors' arithmetic from 'half'), the two arrangements reported as not significantly different without numbers; no test statistics printed.

set.plain: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely? Maybe, but in people nobody has tested it properly. The idea comes from learning: the place, the people and the ritual that usually come with a drug start to trigger the body's own push-back against it, and that push-back is part of tolerance, so tolerance may be weaker where the drug isn't usually taken. In the rat experiment we read, both rooms were familiar to the rats: each rat had heroin in one room and dummy injections of sugar water in the other. A large dose then killed about 64 in 100 rats in the room linked with the dummy injections, against about 32 in 100 in the room linked with heroin, and 96 in 100 rats that had never had heroin. So it tested a room linked with the drug, not a new place. Nobody measured the rats' tolerance, only whether they died, and rats aren't people. The only study in people asked 10 overdose survivors in methadone treatment in New York, about 5 years later, what had been different that day. Seven recalled something unusual, but only 3 meant a new place or crowd; 2 meant a different way of injecting and 2 a different mix of drugs, and 3 recalled nothing unusual. Nobody compared these days with the same people's ordinary days, or counted how often people use somewhere new without overdosing, so the study can't show a higher risk. A treatment based on the idea was proposed without any trial.
set.population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the one animal experiment read, 107 male Wistar-derived laboratory rats aged 90 to 110 days with no opioid experience at the start (37, 42 and 28 per group; editors' sum); in the other animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
set.exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one); in the rat experiment, a single high intravenous heroin dose (15 mg/kg; study condition) given in the setting that had been paired with inactive dextrose injections, after 15 rising doses of heroin on alternate days in the other setting, both settings being familiar
set.comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, rats with the same heroin history given the same test dose in the setting previously paired with heroin, and rats with no previous opioid that had had inactive injections in both settings
set.outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in the rat experiment, death within minutes of a single high intravenous dose (tolerance itself not measured); in the review's other animal work, tolerance and death after a high dose
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The human evidence is a case series (card sc_siegel_1984: JBI prevalence checklist, high risk): 10 survivors from one clinic, chosen in an unreported way, recalling the occasion about 5 years later in open-ended interviews, with the accounts sorted by the author without stated definitions or a second rater; with no comparison occasions and no comparison group, a count of 7 of 10 cannot estimate any risk. The one rat experiment read (card sc_siegel_1982: SYRCLE, high risk) reports no method of allocation, no blinding, no losses and no test statistics, and its printed p value for the main comparison does not reproduce from its counts; the other animal work is described by its author without figures (card sc_siegel_2005: a short narrative review of his own research programme, high risk).
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: The evidence that setting changes the chance of dying is from one rat experiment, which compared a heroin-paired setting with a familiar setting paired with an inactive injection (not a new place) and measured death, not tolerance; the human study interviewed survivors only, although its abstract extends the idea to deaths, and its unusual circumstances include changes of injection and of drug combination that the rat experiment did not test; the human laboratory examples concern alcohol and caffeine, not opioids or overdose.
set.grade.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author's group: one rat experiment, read in full (Siegel et al., 1982), and other animal work described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005). In the rat experiment a high test dose killed about twice as many rats in the setting paired with an inactive injection as in the setting paired with heroin (27 of 42 against 12 of 37, editors' counts); both settings were familiar to every rat, death was the only outcome, tolerance was not measured, and the printed significance of the difference is overstated (p about .005 rather than < .001, editors' calculation). These findings show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings; they are not evidence about people, they concern a place linked with the drug rather than a new place, and they do not raise the rating. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 1982 experiment is in rats, and the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite the 1984 interviews).

evidence_add.locator: Report text without headings, paragraphs counted from the first after the abstract: 6th and 7th paragraphs (p. 437, left column); notes 16 and 17 (p. 437)
evidence_add.extracted: Opiate-inexperienced male Wistar-derived rats aged 90 to 110 days, with permanent jugular cannulas, received 15 intravenous heroin injections, one every other day (1 mg/kg once, 2 mg/kg twice, 4 mg/kg four times, then 8 mg/kg eight times; study conditions), and a volume-matched injection of the vehicle, 5% dextrose, on the days between. Injections were given in two settings: the colony, where rats were housed singly and were taken out, injected and put back; and a different room with constant white noise (60 dB SPL), where rats were injected 15 minutes after arriving and kept 2 more hours. One group had heroin in the distinctive room and dextrose in the colony, the other the reverse, so every rat knew both settings. All were then given 15 mg/kg of heroin either in the setting that had signalled the earlier heroin doses (similarly tested, ST) or in the setting that had not (differently tested, DT), both groups having had the same doses at the same intervals. Of the 37 ST rats, 17 were tested in the distinctive room and 20 in the colony, and half of the 42 DT rats in each; the two counterbalanced arrangements are reported as not significantly different, without numbers. Control rats had 30 daily dextrose injections alternating between the two settings and no opioid before the same test dose. Infusions ran at 0.005 mL/s through the cannula by pump, about 1 minute per kg at every dose.

evidence_add.extracted: Mortality after the 15 mg/kg test injection: ST 32.4% of 37 rats, DT 64.3% of 42, control 96.4% of 28 (Table 1). Editors' counts, the only whole numbers that give these percentages: 12 of 37, 27 of 42 and 27 of 28 (107 rats, editors' sum; the paper gives no total). Mortality differed among the groups (chi-square, P < .001); both heroin-experienced groups survived the dose more often than controls (P < .002); mortality was higher in DT than in ST rats (P < .001); in each of six replications (three with testing in each setting) a greater proportion of DT than ST rats died (P < .02, binomial test). Among rats that died, the median time from the start of the injection to death (no heartbeat) was 187 s in ST, 174 s in DT and 164 s in control rats, not significantly different. Editors' calculation for DT against ST: difference 31.9 percentage points; risk ratio 1.98 (Katz 95% CI 1.18 to 3.32).

evidence_add.extracted: Death was the only outcome: no breathing, blood level or other measure of tolerance was taken at any point. The authors propose a model of overdose deaths in which tolerance fails where the drug is given in an environment not previously associated with it, describe the design as a methodologically rigorous demonstration of the contribution of contextual stimuli to tolerance, read the DT-ST difference as showing that identical drug histories need not produce equal tolerance to heroin's lethal effect, and conclude that rats given the high dose among cues previously associated with lower doses were more likely to survive than rats given it among cues not associated with the drug. The abstract says the results suggest that conditioned drug-anticipatory responses, besides pharmacological factors, affect heroin-induced mortality. No human data are reported.
